title: UK Picks Tekever AR5 to Replace Watchkeeper as Ukraine's Fire Point Scales to 100 Cruise Missiles a Month
subhead: Two procurement signals dominate today: Britain's MoD selected the Portuguese AR5 for its CORVUS army surveillance program, and Ukrainian missile-maker Fire Point confirmed it now builds around 100 Flamingo cruise missiles monthly. Separately, the US House voted $500M in Taiwan military financing even as President Trump continues to withhold a $14B weapons package.

sections.heading: UK MoD Selects Tekever AR5 for CORVUS, Retiring the Troubled Watchkeeper
sections.body: The UK Ministry of Defence has selected Portugal's Tekever to replace the British Army's fleet of Thales Watchkeeper uncrewed aircraft systems, awarding the company the CORVUS surveillance program. Tekever will supply its AR5, a twin-boom fixed-wing drone, with 20-24 aircraft expected to be delivered by 2029, according to the MoD and company statements carried by Defense News and UK press. Defence Secretary John Healey inspected an AR5 at Tekever's manufacturing plant in Swindon as the deal was announced. The AR5, battle-proven in Ukraine, replaces a Watchkeeper fleet that has been plagued by availability problems since entering service.
sections.whyItMatters: Britain is swapping a heavier, troubled legacy ISR platform for a lighter, commercially-built European drone, a shift toward faster, cheaper and more exportable unmanned surveillance after lessons from Ukraine.

sections.heading: Ukraine's Fire Point Ramps Flamingo Cruise Missile Production
sections.body: Ukrainian missile-maker Fire Point is now producing about 100 Flamingo cruise missiles a month and hundreds of drones daily, according to CEO Iryna Terekh in an interview with The Guardian. The company has developed its own turbojet engine for the Flamingo over a six-month collaboration with a design bureau, and the missile carries a 1,150-kilogram warhead, enough for long-range strikes deep inside Russia. Reuters separately reported the company aims to reach roughly three missiles a day by year-end, matching Russia's production pace. Fire Point has also secured agreements from more than a dozen European defense firms to supply radar, guidance and other systems for its Freyja missile-defense project.
sections.whyItMatters: Ukrainian domestic missile production at this scale is shifting the war's industrial balance — Kyiv can now sustain deep-strike operations without depending solely on Western long-range munitions, and is attracting European suppliers into its own defense-industrial base.

sections.heading: US House Votes $500M for Taiwan as Trump Holds Back $14B Package
sections.body: The US House of Representatives passed a fiscal-year 2027 appropriations bill that includes $500 million in military funding for Taiwan and provisions supporting Taipei's participation in international organizations, Taiwan News reports. The vote signals Congressional willingness to back Taiwan's defense even as President Trump continues to withhold approval of a $14 billion weapons package for the island, which he pulled back in May. The split between Congress and the White House leaves a large tranche of approved-for-sale hardware — from air-defense and munitions to platforms — in limbo while Beijing watches closely.
sections.whyItMatters: The disconnect between a House voting money for Taiwan and a president sitting on a much larger arms sale creates genuine uncertainty over the pace and reliability of US arms deliveries to Taipei, a central variable in cross-strait deterrence.

sections.heading: GAO Finds Only 25% of US F-35s Fully Mission Capable
sections.body: A new Government Accountability Office report found that only 25 percent of US F-35s were fully mission capable through fiscal 2025, with readiness continuing to decline as the Pentagon's most expensive program contends with sustainment and maintenance shortfalls, per Defense One and Forbes. The GAO assessment arrives as partner nations fund a reset — Australia, as an F-35 partner, is contributing $1.44 billion to the fleet recovery effort. The report underscores that after nearly 30 years, the Joint Strike Fighter's sustainment model remains its weakest link even as the US fields the aircraft at scale alongside the new long-range AIM-424 Malice air-to-air missile unveiled this week.
sections.whyItMatters: A 25% full-mission-capable rate challenges the assumption that the F-35 can fight a sustained high-end war as currently sustained; it also raises cost-sharing tensions among the growing number of partner nations pouring money into fixes.

sections.heading: German Arms Exports to Israel Surge ~€800M in Five Months, Tied to Submarine Work
sections.body: Germany approved almost 800 million euros ($913 million) in arms export licences to Israel in the first five months of 2026 — more than in the previous 20 months combined, according to a Federal Foreign Office response to a parliamentary inquiry filed by the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party. A significant portion of the approvals is tied to a submarine project, and the figures do not appear to include naval vessels, per reporting on the disclosure. A Berlin court separately dismissed a Palestinian bid to halt the exports. The surge deepens the German-Israeli defense relationship even as Berlin faces domestic and regional criticism over weapons flowing to a country engaged in multi-front military operations.
sections.whyItMatters: The submarine-linked jump shows Berlin's defense exports to Israel are now a major, structural line of the German defense-industrial order — and a politically fraught one — rather than an occasional approval.

sections.heading: European Sixth-Gen Effort Reforms: 'Team Gen 6' Emerges After FCAS Collapse
sections.body: Following the collapse of the Franco-German Future Combat Air System (FCAS), a new German-led initiative is taking shape: an eight-company consortium dubbed 'Team Gen 6' led by Airbus, according to European defense reporting. Spain's industry is pressing for inclusion in a new European fighter project after the FCAS breakup, per El Pais. Separately, India confirmed to parliament it is in talks with France on joining FCAS as a sixth-generation fighter partner, and Britain's MoD has begun a 'concerted' push to join the French-led program — a sign the European sixth-gen landscape is fragmenting and re-forming around competing poles as Paris and Berlin go separate ways.
sections.whyItMatters: The post-FCAS scramble is redrawing Europe's fighter-industrial map — with Germany building its own consortium, France courting India and the UK, and Spain choosing sides — which will shape the continent's air-power industrial base for decades.

sections.heading: India Picks Meprolight Optic; Russia Bolsters Northern Flank as NATO Responds
sections.body: The Indian Army has selected Israel's Meprolight MEPRO X6 telescopic sight as the dedicated daytime optic for its in-service Negev 7.62×51 light machine guns, a contract valued at Rs 64.31 crore following a multi-year tender, per ANI and Indian defense media. Separately, satellite imagery and reporting show Russia is pulling air-defense systems from Arctic positions while building large new bases near the Finnish and Norwegian borders, even as NATO bolsters its own Arctic combat force — a quiet but significant buildup along the alliance's northern flank.
sections.whyItMatters: India's optics award extends the deepening Israeli presence in Indian Army small-arms modernization, while the Arctic base construction signals Moscow is preparing a northern-front infrastructure footprint that NATO is now racing to match.

bottomLine: Today's news is dominated by industrial capacity: Britain committing to a fast, commercially-built European drone to replace a legacy fleet, and Ukraine scaling domestic cruise-missile output to a pace that rivals Russia's. On the procurement front, Congress and the White House are visibly out of step on Taiwan arming, Germany is quietly expanding submarine-linked exports to Israel, and a fresh GAO finding — only a quarter of US F-35s fully mission capable — puts a spotlight on the readiness bill coming due across the alliance. Europe's sixth-generation fighter project is fragmenting into competing consortia, reshaping who builds the continent's next air power. None of these are single-day turning points; together they describe a defense order where production capacity and sustainment, not just platform announcements, are the binding constraints.
sources: Defense News, UK Ministry of Defence, Tekever, The Guardian, Reuters, Ukrinform, Taiwan News, Defense One, Forbes, GAO, Federal Foreign Office of Germany (via parliamentary inquiry), AfD, El Pais, ANI, Indian defense media, Bing News aggregations
